excerpt: The Frontier Safety Framework is a set of protocols that aims to address severe risks that may arise from the high-impact capabilities of frontier AI models.
paraphrase: The Framework is a set of protocols targeting severe risks from frontier AI models' high-impact capabilities.

excerpt: It complements Google's suite of AI responsibility and safety practices, and enables Google's AI innovation and deployment consistent with our AI Principles.
paraphrase: The Framework complements Google's broader safety practices and supports AI innovation consistent with its AI Principles.

excerpt: The Framework is informed by the broader conversation on Frontier AI Safety and Security Frameworks.
paraphrase: The Framework draws on the wider discourse regarding Frontier AI Safety and Security Frameworks.

excerpt: The core components of such Frameworks are to:
paraphrase: This introduces a list of core components of such Frameworks.

context_stem: The core components of such Frameworks are to:
excerpt: Identify capability levels at which frontier AI models, without additional mitigations, could pose severe risk.
paraphrase: One core component is identifying capability levels that could pose severe risk absent mitigations.

context_stem: The core components of such Frameworks are to:
excerpt: Implement protocols to detect the attainment of such capability levels throughout the model lifecycle.
paraphrase: Another core component is implementing detection protocols throughout the model's lifecycle.

context_stem: The core components of such Frameworks are to:
excerpt: Prepare and articulate proactive mitigation plans to ensure severe risks are adequately mitigated when such capability levels are attained.
paraphrase: Another core component is preparing proactive mitigation plans for when capability levels are reached.

context_stem: The core components of such Frameworks are to:
excerpt: Where required or appropriate, involve external parties to help inform and guide the approach.
paraphrase: Another core component is involving external parties when required or appropriate.

excerpt: In the Framework, we specify protocols for the detection of capability levels at which frontier AI models may pose significant or severe risks (which we call "Tracked Capability Levels (TCLs)" and "Critical Capability Levels (CCLs)" respectively), and articulate mitigation approaches to address such risks.
paraphrase: The Framework specifies detection protocols for TCLs and CCLs and articulates mitigation approaches for them.

excerpt: The Framework addresses misuse risk as well as machine learning research and development (ML R&D) and misalignment risk.
paraphrase: The Framework covers misuse risk as well as ML R&D and misalignment risk.

excerpt: For each type of risk, we define a set of CCLs (and TCLs where relevant) and a mitigation approach for them.
paraphrase: For each risk type, the Framework defines CCLs, TCLs where relevant, and a mitigation approach.

excerpt: Risk assessment will necessarily involve evaluating cross-cutting capabilities such as agency, tool use, reasoning, and scientific understanding.
paraphrase: Risk assessment necessarily requires evaluating cross-cutting capabilities such as agency, tool use, reasoning, and scientific understanding.

excerpt: Please refer to the Glossary at the end of this document for definitions used in the Framework.
paraphrase: Readers are directed to the Glossary for defined terms.

excerpt: The safety and security of frontier AI models is a global public good.
paraphrase: Frontier AI model safety and security is characterized as a global public good.

excerpt: The protocols here represent our current understanding and approach of how severe frontier AI risks may be anticipated and addressed.
paraphrase: These protocols reflect the current understanding of anticipating and addressing severe frontier AI risks.

excerpt: Importantly, there are certain mitigations whose social value is significantly reduced if not broadly applied to frontier AI models reaching critical capabilities.
paraphrase: Some mitigations lose much of their social value unless broadly applied across frontier AI models at critical capabilities.

excerpt: These mitigations are most effective when adopted by industry as a whole: our adoption of them would result in effective risk mitigation for society only if all relevant organizations provide similar levels of protection.
paraphrase: Such mitigations are most effective as an industry-wide practice, since Google's adoption alone would not ensure societal risk mitigation.

excerpt: The Framework is based on early and evolving research.
paraphrase: The Framework rests on research that is early-stage and still evolving.

excerpt: We may change our approach over time as we gain experience and insights on the projected capabilities of future frontier models.
paraphrase: The approach may change as more experience and insight into future model capabilities is gained.

excerpt: We will review the Framework periodically and we expect it to evolve substantially as our understanding of the risks and benefits of frontier models improves.
paraphrase: The Framework will be reviewed periodically and is expected to change substantially as understanding improves.

excerpt: See https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/emerging-processes-for-frontier-ai-safety, https://metr.org/faisc, https://www.anthropic.com/rsp-updates, https://www.anthropic.com/news/compliance-framework-SB53, https://openai.com/index/updating-our-preparedness-framework/, https://www.frontiermodelforum.org/publications/#technical-reports.
paraphrase: Footnote lists external resources on frontier AI safety and security frameworks.

excerpt: As in, in the context of the Framework, risks of threat actors using critical capabilities of deployed or exfiltrated models to cause harm.
paraphrase: Footnote clarifies misuse risk means threat actors leveraging deployed or exfiltrated model capabilities to cause harm.

excerpt: In the context of the Framework, we address specific scenarios where model misalignment may create the risk of significant or severe harm, and scenarios where ML R&D capabilities may heighten misalignment, misuse, and structural risks.
paraphrase: Footnote explains that the Framework addresses misalignment scenarios and ML R&D capabilities that heighten various risks.

excerpt: This section describes the central components of the Frontier Safety Framework.
paraphrase: This section introduces the central components of the Framework.

excerpt: These protocols represent our current understanding of and approach for how severe frontier AI risks may be anticipated and addressed.
paraphrase: The protocols reflect the current understanding of anticipating and addressing severe frontier AI risks.

excerpt: The Frontier Safety Framework focuses on possible severe risks stemming from high-impact capabilities of frontier AI models.
paraphrase: The Framework's focus is possible severe risks from high-impact frontier AI capabilities.

excerpt: The Framework complements Google's suite of AI responsibility and safety practices, which address other risks in addition to the severe risks in scope of the Framework in accordance with our AI Principles.
paraphrase: The Framework complements broader AI responsibility and safety practices covering additional risks, in line with AI Principles.

excerpt: The approaches and mitigations outlined in the Framework are not exclusive to models where we believe a severe risk could arise and are part of Google's comprehensive AI responsibility and safety practices.
paraphrase: The Framework's approaches and mitigations apply beyond just models believed to pose severe risk, as part of comprehensive safety practices.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
excerpt: The Framework is built primarily around capability thresholds called "Critical Capability Levels (CCLs)."
paraphrase: CCLs are the primary capability thresholds structuring the Framework.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
excerpt: These are capability levels at which, absent mitigation measures, frontier AI models or systems may pose heightened risk of severe harm.
paraphrase: CCLs are levels where models could pose heightened severe-harm risk without mitigations.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
excerpt: CCLs are determined by identifying and analyzing the main foreseeable paths through which a model could result in severe harm: we then define the CCLs as the minimal set of capabilities a model must possess to do so.
paraphrase: CCLs are derived from analyzing foreseeable paths to severe harm and defining the minimal capabilities needed.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
excerpt: CCLs are one important component of our risk acceptance determination.
paraphrase: CCLs feed into the risk acceptance determination process.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
excerpt: We identify CCLs for two kinds of risks: misuse risk and risks related to machine learning R&D and misalignment.
paraphrase: CCLs are defined for misuse risk and for ML R&D/misalignment risk.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
excerpt: For misuse risk, we define CCLs in the following risk domains where the misuse of model capabilities may result in severe harm:
paraphrase: This introduces the misuse risk domains for which CCLs are defined.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
context_stem: For misuse risk, we define CCLs in the following risk domains where the misuse of model capabilities may result in severe harm:
excerpt: CBRN: Risks of models assisting in the development, preparation, and/or execution of a chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear ("CBRN") threat.
paraphrase: CBRN domain covers risks of models assisting CBRN threats.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
context_stem: For misuse risk, we define CCLs in the following risk domains where the misuse of model capabilities may result in severe harm:
excerpt: Cyber: Risks of models assisting in the development, preparation, and/or execution of a cyber attack.
paraphrase: Cyber domain covers risks of models assisting cyber attacks.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
context_stem: For misuse risk, we define CCLs in the following risk domains where the misuse of model capabilities may result in severe harm:
excerpt: Harmful Manipulation: Risks of models with high manipulative capabilities potentially being misused in ways that could reasonably result in large scale harm.
paraphrase: Harmful Manipulation domain covers risks from highly manipulative models being misused to cause large scale harm.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
excerpt: For machine learning R&D and misalignment risks, we define CCLs that identify when ML R&D capabilities in our models may, if not properly managed, reduce society's overall ability to manage AI risks.
paraphrase: For ML R&D and misalignment risks, CCLs identify when unmanaged capabilities could reduce society's ability to manage AI risks.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
excerpt: Such capabilities may serve as a substantial cross-cutting risk factor for several pathways (e.g. through misalignment, misuse or structural risks) to severe harm.
paraphrase: These capabilities can be a cross-cutting risk factor across multiple pathways to severe harm.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
excerpt: This update to the Framework introduces "Tracked Capability Levels (TCLs)."
paraphrase: This version introduces the new concept of Tracked Capability Levels (TCLs).

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
excerpt: TCLs are meant to capture significant risks that may manifest at a lower capability threshold than our CCLs and we apply our mitigation and risk acceptance determination process proportionately.
paraphrase: TCLs capture significant risks at lower thresholds than CCLs, with mitigation applied proportionately.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
excerpt: We identify TCLs for CBRN risk, as well as ML R&D and misalignment risks.
paraphrase: TCLs are identified for CBRN risk and ML R&D/misalignment risks.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
excerpt: We may include TCLs for additional risks in the future, as our threat modeling develops.
paraphrase: Additional TCLs may be added in the future as threat modeling evolves.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
excerpt: Similarly to CCLs, early warning evaluations will be used to assess the proximity of a model to a TCL and analyze the risk posed, involving internal and external experts as needed.
paraphrase: As with CCLs, early warning evaluations assess proximity to a TCL and involve internal/external experts as needed.

excerpt: We conduct our risk management process as appropriate, throughout the model development process, on various checkpoints or versions of a model, both before and after deployment.
paraphrase: The risk management process is applied throughout model development, across checkpoints, before and after deployment.

excerpt: The first part of our risk management process is risk identification.
paraphrase: Risk identification is the initial stage of the risk management process.

excerpt: We identify potential risks that could stem from our models and analyze their characteristics to determine which of the identified risks could be significant or severe risks.
paraphrase: Potential risks from models are identified and analyzed to determine which are significant or severe.

excerpt: We consider a wide range of risks as part of our ongoing research, taking into account the characteristics, capabilities, propensities, and affordances of our models and other sources of information, such as our internal risk taxonomies, internal expertise and relevant external research.
paraphrase: A wide range of risks are considered using model characteristics and various information sources including internal taxonomies and external research.

excerpt: As explained above, we have identified risk domains where, based on early research, we have determined significant or severe risks may be most likely to arise from future models: CBRN, cyber, harmful manipulation, as well as machine learning R&D and misalignment.
paraphrase: Identified risk domains most likely to produce significant or severe risk are CBRN, cyber, harmful manipulation, and ML R&D/misalignment.

excerpt: As part of our broader research into and development of frontier AI models, we continue to assess whether there are other risk domains where significant or severe risks may arise and will update our approach as appropriate.
paraphrase: Ongoing research continues to assess whether other risk domains exist, with the approach updated as appropriate.

excerpt: For each of the four identified domains, we have developed specific scenarios and T/CCLs in which these risks could materialize.
paraphrase: Specific scenarios and T/CCLs have been developed for each of the four risk domains.

excerpt: To understand whether a model may, without appropriate mitigations, contribute to the risks identified, we conduct a closer assessment of its capabilities against the T/CCLs.
paraphrase: A closer capability assessment against T/CCLs is conducted to gauge whether a model could contribute to identified risks without mitigations.

excerpt: We conduct a critical capability assessment prior to the first external deployment of a new frontier AI model.
paraphrase: A critical capability assessment occurs before first external deployment of a new frontier model.

excerpt: For external deployment of subsequent versions of the model, we determine whether a substantial modification has been made and whether a further critical capability assessment is required if (1) the model has meaningful new capabilities or material increases in performance; and (2) we believe such material capability increase could materially undermine the justification for why the risks stemming from the model are acceptable.
paraphrase: For subsequent versions, a further critical capability assessment is required if there are meaningful new capabilities or material performance increases that could undermine the prior risk-acceptability justification.

excerpt: To understand if a subsequent version of the model has meaningful new capabilities or material increases in performance relative to the last checkpoint subject to a critical capability assessment, we conduct material capability change assessments on various checkpoints upon the completion of a post-training run.
paraphrase: Material capability change assessments are conducted on checkpoints after post-training runs to compare against the last assessed checkpoint.

excerpt: These assessments draw on model characteristics, such as its provenance, size, modality, and performance on general capability benchmarks.
paraphrase: Assessments use model characteristics including provenance, size, modality, and general benchmark performance.

excerpt: To understand if such a change in capability in the subsequent version of the model could materially undermine the justification for why the risks stemming from the model are acceptable, we may also conduct light-weight versions of our "early warning evaluations" described below, including our automated benchmarks, to confirm a model remains below T/CCL.
paraphrase: Light-weight early warning evaluations, including automated benchmarks, may be conducted to confirm a model remains below T/CCL.

excerpt: We may also apply material capability change assessments to models not on the frontier, to understand whether a critical capability assessment is required.
paraphrase: Material capability change assessments may also apply to non-frontier models to determine whether a critical capability assessment is needed.

excerpt: Central to our critical capability assessments are "early warning evaluations," which we use to test the specific threats and risk scenarios identified through our threat modeling, determine a model's capability, and assess the proximity of the model to a T/CCL.
paraphrase: Early warning evaluations are central to critical capability assessments, testing threat scenarios and assessing proximity to a T/CCL.

excerpt: For CCLs, we define "alert thresholds," which may draw on evaluation results, expert assessments, and other sources of information; that are designed to flag when a CCL may be reached before a critical capability assessment is conducted again.
paraphrase: Alert thresholds are defined for CCLs, drawing on multiple information sources, to flag possible CCL attainment before the next assessment.

excerpt: In our evaluations, we seek to apply appropriate scaffolding, inference compute, and other augmentations to also assess the capabilities of systems that will likely be produced with the model based on the specific threats and risk scenarios we have identified for the T/CCL.
paraphrase: Evaluations aim to apply scaffolding, inference compute, and other augmentations to assess likely downstream systems based on identified threat scenarios.

excerpt: We may run early warning evaluations more frequently or adjust alert thresholds if the rate of progress suggests our safety buffer is no longer adequate.
paraphrase: Early warning evaluations may be run more often, or alert thresholds adjusted, if progress suggests the safety buffer is insufficient.

excerpt: We conduct further analysis, including reviewing model-independent information, external evaluations, and post-market monitoring as appropriate.
paraphrase: Further analysis is conducted, including reviewing model-independent information, external evaluations, and post-market monitoring as appropriate.

excerpt: In particular, we strive to learn from our post-market monitoring mechanisms, including as part of our detection, mitigation, response and/or reporting of incidents relating to our frontier safety risk domains.
paraphrase: There is an effort to learn from post-market monitoring mechanisms related to detecting, mitigating, responding to, and reporting incidents in frontier safety risk domains.

excerpt: Actionable insights from these processes allow us to enhance our tools, training, processes, policies, and response efforts.
paraphrase: Insights from these processes are used to enhance tools, training, processes, policies, and response efforts.

excerpt: Our approach to model evaluations and inherent risk assessments described above means we can proactively monitor a model's capabilities throughout the entire lifecycle of the model and ensure that any significant or severe risk is properly identified and mitigated.
paraphrase: This approach allows proactive lifecycle-wide monitoring and ensures significant or severe risks are identified and mitigated.

excerpt: Where appropriate, we may engage relevant external actors, including governments, to inform our responsible development and deployment practices.
paraphrase: External actors, including governments, may be engaged where appropriate to inform responsible development and deployment practices.

excerpt: Note on Machine Learning R&D CCLs: Risk assessment must take into account the fact that other actors may put significantly more effort into eliciting capabilities than we put into assessing risk, thus requiring conservatism in the form of evaluations.
paraphrase: For ML R&D CCLs, risk assessment must account for other actors potentially putting more effort into eliciting capabilities, requiring conservative evaluation.

excerpt: However, as a frontier AI company, we do not expect other groups to put significantly more effort into ML R&D than we do ourselves.
paraphrase: As a frontier AI company, it is not expected that other groups would exceed its own effort in ML R&D.

excerpt: As a result, to assess the ML R&D CCLs, we may use sources of information about our own progress at accelerating ML R&D to assess whether we are near or at the ML R&D CCLs, in addition to evaluations of ML R&D capabilities.
paraphrase: ML R&D CCL assessment may draw on information about internal ML R&D acceleration progress in addition to capability evaluations.

excerpt: A critical capability assessment may not be conducted for low-risk external deployments (e.g. to a small number of trusted testers) if the appropriate governance function determines the residual risk of such deployments to be acceptable even if the model has reached a T/CCL (including with a safety case where a CCL has been reached).
paraphrase: Low-risk external deployments may skip a critical capability assessment if governance deems residual risk acceptable, even at T/CCL, with a safety case for CCLs.

excerpt: We apply safety and security mitigations throughout the lifecycle of our models, including as part of our training and model development phase and, where appropriate, before T/CCLs are reached as described in the process below.
paraphrase: Safety and security mitigations apply across a model's lifecycle, including training/development, and before T/CCLs are reached where appropriate.

excerpt: When a model reaches an alert threshold for a CCL, we will assess the proximity of the model to the CCL and analyze the risk posed, involving internal and external experts as needed.
paraphrase: Reaching an alert threshold for a CCL triggers assessment of proximity and risk, involving experts as needed.

excerpt: This will inform the formulation and application of a response plan.
paraphrase: The assessment informs formulation and application of a response plan.

excerpt: Central to most response plans will be the application of the mitigations described later in the Framework.
paraphrase: Most response plans center on applying the mitigations described later in the Framework.

excerpt: However, if we assess that risks stemming from the model remain acceptable and model capabilities remain distant from a CCL, the response plan may include updating the alert threshold to ensure the safety buffer remains appropriate.
paraphrase: If risks remain acceptable and capabilities are distant from a CCL, the response plan may instead update the alert threshold to keep the safety buffer appropriate.

excerpt: We have two categories of mitigations: security mitigations (such as preventing the exfiltration of model weights), and deployment mitigations (such as safety fine-tuning and monitoring and response) intended to counter the misuse or misaligned expression of critical capabilities in deployments.
paraphrase: There are two mitigation categories: security mitigations (e.g., preventing weight exfiltration) and deployment mitigations (e.g., safety fine-tuning, monitoring) to counter misuse or misaligned expression in deployments.

excerpt: The mitigations described in this document are limited to those mitigations that will be required to bring a model to an acceptable level of risk relative just to the specific T/CCL, which by definition pose the greatest risks of harm.
paraphrase: Described mitigations are limited to those needed to bring a model to acceptable risk relative to the specific T/CCL, which represents the greatest harm risks.

excerpt: Because we cannot always anticipate what security and deployment mitigations will be appropriate for models beyond the current frontier, the specific mitigations we implement may be determined when a T/CCL is reached, informed by the threat landscape at that time.
paraphrase: Since future appropriate mitigations cannot always be anticipated, specific mitigations may be determined at the time a T/CCL is reached, informed by the then-current threat landscape.

excerpt: These mitigations also reflect considerations from the perspective of addressing significant and severe risks from powerful capabilities alone; due to this focused scope, other risk management and security considerations may result in more stringent mitigations applied to a model than specified by the Framework.
paraphrase: The mitigations reflect a focused scope on powerful-capability risks; other considerations may lead to more stringent mitigations than the Framework specifies.

excerpt: We will use various processes to evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of mitigations:
paraphrase: Multiple processes are used to evaluate mitigation effectiveness and limitations.

context_stem: We will use various processes to evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of mitigations:
excerpt: Security mitigations: security infrastructure at Google is subject to penetration testing and other kinds of assessments, and is continually improved based on these results.
paraphrase: Security infrastructure undergoes penetration testing and other assessments, and is continually improved based on results.

context_stem: We will use various processes to evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of mitigations:
excerpt: Deployment mitigations: we will use a combination of threat modeling, empirical testing, and other sources of information to assess the effectiveness and limitations of our deployment mitigations.
paraphrase: Deployment mitigations are assessed using threat modeling, empirical testing, and other information sources.

excerpt: Models reaching TCLs or CCLs will be subject to residual risk assessments as part of evaluating their deployment mitigations.
paraphrase: Models that reach TCLs or CCLs undergo residual risk assessments as part of deployment mitigation evaluation.

excerpt: For models reaching CCLs, the residual risk assessment will be informed by a supplemental safety case.
paraphrase: A supplemental safety case informs the residual risk assessment for models reaching CCLs.

excerpt: See the deployment mitigations sections below regarding misuse and machine learning R&D and misalignment for more.
paraphrase: Further detail is available in the later deployment mitigations sections on misuse and ML R&D/misalignment.

excerpt: The Framework outlines the risk acceptance determination approach for different model risks and capabilities pertaining to significant and severe risks.
paraphrase: The Framework sets out the risk acceptance determination approach across different model risks and capabilities.

excerpt: A model for which inherent risk assessment indicates no T/CCL is reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of risk for further development and deployment, because it should not possess the capabilities required to substantially contribute to significant or severe risk scenarios.
paraphrase: Models not reaching any T/CCL are deemed acceptable risk for further development and deployment, since they lack capabilities for significant or severe risk scenarios.

excerpt: A model for which the inherent risk assessment indicates a misuse T/CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of residual risk for further development or deployment, if:
paraphrase: A model that reaches a misuse T/CCL is deemed acceptable residual risk for further development or deployment only if certain conditions apply.

context_stem: A model for which the inherent risk assessment indicates a misuse T/CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of residual risk for further development or deployment, if:
excerpt: We assess that the deployment mitigations have brought the residual risk of harm to an acceptable level, based on considerations such as the effectiveness of mitigations, the scope of the deployment, what capabilities and mitigations are available on other publicly available models (e.g. if other models are similarly capable and have few mitigations, then the marginal risk added by our external deployment is likely low), and the historical incidence and severity of related events.
paraphrase: Deployment mitigations must be assessed as bringing residual harm risk to an acceptable level, considering mitigation effectiveness, deployment scope, comparator model capabilities/mitigations, and historical event severity.

context_stem: A model for which the inherent risk assessment indicates a misuse T/CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of residual risk for further development or deployment, if:
excerpt: This is required only for external deployment, not internal deployment or further development.
paraphrase: This deployment mitigation condition applies only to external deployment, not internal deployment or further development.

context_stem: A model for which the inherent risk assessment indicates a misuse T/CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of residual risk for further development or deployment, if:
excerpt: Security mitigations have been applied to the model weights reaching the recommended security level stated below, or we otherwise assess that the level of security applied is adequate, e.g. based on mitigations already in place, if they match or exceed the level of security applied to other models with similar capabilities or risk profiles, or we assess that the benefits of the open release of model weights outweigh the risks.
paraphrase: Security mitigations must reach the recommended security level, or the applied security level must be assessed adequate relative to comparator models, or the benefits of open release must be assessed to outweigh risks.

excerpt: A model for which the inherent risk assessment indicates a ML R&D CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of residual risk for further development or deployment, if:
paraphrase: A model reaching an ML R&D CCL is deemed acceptable residual risk for further development or deployment only if certain conditions apply.

context_stem: A model for which the inherent risk assessment indicates a ML R&D CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of residual risk for further development or deployment, if:
excerpt: We assess that the deployment mitigations have brought the residual risk of severe harm to an acceptable level, based on considerations such as the effectiveness of mitigations, and information pertaining to model propensities and the severity of related events.
paraphrase: Deployment mitigations must be assessed as bringing severe harm residual risk to an acceptable level, based on mitigation effectiveness, model propensities, and event severity.

context_stem: A model for which the inherent risk assessment indicates a ML R&D CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of residual risk for further development or deployment, if:
excerpt: This is required only for external deployment and high-risk internal deployment, not further development.
paraphrase: This condition applies only to external deployment and high-risk internal deployment, not further development.

context_stem: A model for which the inherent risk assessment indicates a ML R&D CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of residual risk for further development or deployment, if:
excerpt: Security mitigations have been applied to the model weights reaching the recommended security level stated below, or we otherwise assess that the level of security applied is adequate, e.g. based on mitigations already in place, if they match or exceed the level of security applied to other models with similar capabilities or risk profiles, or we assess that the benefits of the open release of model weights outweigh the risks.
paraphrase: Security mitigations must reach the recommended level, or be otherwise assessed adequate relative to comparator models, or the benefits of open release must outweigh the risks.

excerpt: Note that deployment mitigations for the ML R&D CCLs are different than those for the misuse CCLs because of differences in which deployment could lead to severe harm for those respective categories.
paraphrase: Footnote clarifies that ML R&D CCL deployment mitigations differ from misuse CCL mitigations due to differing harm pathways.

excerpt: In contrast, security mitigations protecting against weights exfiltration and unauthorized modification are generally beneficial to both kinds of risk.
paraphrase: Footnote notes that security mitigations against exfiltration and unauthorized modification benefit both risk categories.

excerpt: A model for which the inherent risk assessment indicates the TCL for ML R&D and misalignment risk has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of residual risk for further development or deployment, if:
paraphrase: A model reaching the ML R&D and misalignment TCL is deemed acceptable residual risk for further development or deployment only if certain conditions apply.

context_stem: A model for which the inherent risk assessment indicates the TCL for ML R&D and misalignment risk has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of residual risk for further development or deployment, if:
excerpt: We assess that the deployment mitigations have brought the residual risk of significant harm to an acceptable level, based on considerations such as the effectiveness of mitigations, and information pertaining to model propensities and the severity of related events, or if we assess that the model is very unlikely to possess the propensities that would be required for material risk of significant harm through misalignment risk.
paraphrase: Deployment mitigations must be assessed as reducing significant harm risk to acceptable levels, or the model must be assessed very unlikely to possess propensities for material misalignment-driven harm.

context_stem: A model for which the inherent risk assessment indicates the TCL for ML R&D and misalignment risk has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of residual risk for further development or deployment, if:
excerpt: This is required only for external deployment and high-risk internal deployment, not further development.
paraphrase: This condition applies only to external deployment and high-risk internal deployment, not further development.

context_stem: A model for which the inherent risk assessment indicates the TCL for ML R&D and misalignment risk has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of residual risk for further development or deployment, if:
excerpt: We assess that the level of security applied is adequate, e.g. based on mitigations already in place, if they match or exceed the level of security applied to other models with similar capabilities or risk profiles, or we assess that the benefits of the open release of model weights outweigh the risks.
paraphrase: Security level must be assessed adequate, e.g., matching or exceeding comparator models, or the benefits of open release must outweigh the risks.

excerpt: Note: Assessing frontier AI capabilities and corresponding significant and severe risk is a complex process.
paraphrase: A note states that assessing frontier AI capabilities and corresponding risk is complex.

excerpt: Because the science of AI risk assessment is still developing, our assessments will often involve some level of subjective analysis.
paraphrase: Since the science of AI risk assessment is still developing, assessments will often involve subjective analysis.

excerpt: The concept of proportionality is central to our determination of whether a particular mitigation has sufficiently reduced the risk to acceptable levels.
paraphrase: Proportionality is central to determining whether a mitigation has sufficiently reduced risk to acceptable levels.

excerpt: The mitigation and the effects of such mitigation should also be assessed holistically and be proportionate with expected impact of a model's risk, thus balancing safety with innovation.
paraphrase: Mitigations and their effects should be assessed holistically and proportionately to expected risk impact, balancing safety with innovation.

excerpt: This section describes our mitigation approach for models that pose risks of significant or severe harm through misuse, and then details our set of misuse T/CCLs (CBRN, cyber and harmful manipulation), as well as the mitigation approach that we assess as appropriate for them.
paraphrase: This section covers the mitigation approach for misuse-related harm, and details the misuse T/CCLs and their appropriate mitigations.

excerpt: There are two categories of mitigations to address models with misuse critical capabilities: security mitigations intended to prevent the exfiltration or unauthorized modification of model weights, and deployment mitigations intended to counter the misuse of critical capabilities in external deployments.
paraphrase: Two mitigation categories address misuse critical capabilities: security mitigations against weight exfiltration/modification, and deployment mitigations against misuse in external deployments.

excerpt: For security, we have several levels of mitigations, allowing calibration of the appropriateness and robustness of security measures to the risks posed.
paraphrase: Multiple security mitigation levels allow calibrating measure robustness to the risks posed.

excerpt: Regarding deployment mitigations for models reaching T/CCLs, we specify a standard process for applying, assessing, and reviewing mitigations: the aim of this process is to calibrate mitigations to T/CCLs, and the procedural approach reflects the more iterative and T/CCL-dependent nature of deployment mitigations.
paraphrase: A standard process governs applying, assessing, and reviewing deployment mitigations for models reaching T/CCLs, aiming to calibrate mitigations to the specific T/CCL given its iterative nature.

excerpt: This structured process for deployment mitigations is centered on assessing and reviewing that the risk of severe harm has been brought to an acceptable level proportionate to the risk.
paraphrase: The structured deployment mitigation process centers on ensuring severe harm risk is reduced to an acceptable, proportionate level.

excerpt: Security mitigations against exfiltration or unauthorized modification risk, such as identity and access management practices and hardening interface-access to unreleased model parameters, are important for models reaching misuse CCLs.
paraphrase: Security mitigations like identity/access management and interface hardening are important for models reaching misuse CCLs.

excerpt: This is because the release or unauthorized modification of model weights may enable the removal of any safeguards trained into or deployed with the model, and hence access (including by threat actors) to any critical capabilities.
paraphrase: Weight release or unauthorized modification could remove trained safeguards, enabling threat actor access to critical capabilities.

excerpt: Using Google's Secure AI Framework (SAIF) and Google's common security infrastructure, we implement state-of-the-art security mitigations.
paraphrase: State-of-the-art security mitigations are implemented using Google's SAIF and common security infrastructure.

excerpt: SAIF is a defense-in-depth approach that embeds security into every layer of our AI systems—from data and infrastructure to models and applications.
paraphrase: SAIF embeds security defense-in-depth across all AI system layers, from data/infrastructure to models/applications.

excerpt: SAIF is premised on six core elements: strong security foundations, detection and response, automated defenses, harmonized platform-level controls, adaptable controls to mitigate emerging threats, and end-to-end risk assessments.
paraphrase: SAIF rests on six core elements including security foundations, detection/response, automated defenses, platform controls, adaptable controls, and end-to-end risk assessments.

excerpt: We use security levels to indicate security goals/principles in line with the corresponding level in the RAND model weight security framework.
paraphrase: Security levels indicate goals/principles aligned with corresponding RAND model weight security framework levels.

excerpt: We also define and recommend "Security Level 2+," which uses RAND Security Level 2 (SL2) as a baseline, with additional security measures designed to address risks from insider threats and well-resourced non-state external actors.
paraphrase: A new "Security Level 2+" is defined, building on RAND SL2 baseline with added measures against insider threats and well-resourced non-state actors.

excerpt: These additional measures may include, for example: dedicated insider risk teams; background checks and ID verification for personnel with sensitive access; review of model training data for signs of tampering; mandating that the processing of untrusted inputs occurs within sandboxed environments; advanced red-teaming that simulates well-resourced adversaries (including Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) groups); and proactive threat hunting with 24/7 incident response capabilities.
paraphrase: Example additional Security Level 2+ measures include insider risk teams, personnel background checks, training data tampering review, sandboxed processing of untrusted inputs, advanced red-teaming against APT-level adversaries, and 24/7 proactive threat hunting.

excerpt: Because AI security is an area of active research, we expect the concrete measures implemented to reach each level of security to evolve substantially.
paraphrase: Since AI security is actively researched, the concrete measures for each security level are expected to evolve substantially.

excerpt: In other words, "security level N" indicates security controls and detections at a level generally aligned with RAND SL N.
paraphrase: Footnote clarifies that "security level N" aligns generally with RAND SL N.

excerpt: See https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA2849-1.html, pp 21-22.
paraphrase: Footnote cites the RAND report pages referenced.

excerpt: In aligning our security levels with RAND's, we are referring to the security goals and principles in the RAND framework, rather than the benchmarks (i.e. concrete measures) also described in the RAND report.
paraphrase: Footnote clarifies alignment is with RAND's goals/principles rather than its concrete benchmark measures.

excerpt: As the authors point out, the "security level benchmarks represent neither a complete standard nor a compliance regime—they are provided for informational purposes only and should inform security teams' decisions rather than supersede them."
paraphrase: Footnote quotes RAND authors stating the benchmarks are informational only, not a complete standard or compliance regime.

excerpt: We set out below a set of CBRN, cyber, and harmful manipulation CCLs as well as the CBRN TCL that we have identified through ongoing analysis of these risk domains. We expect these to evolve over time.

excerpt: These recommended security levels reflect our current thinking proportionate to the risks posed and may be adjusted if our understanding of the risks changes.

excerpt: This may occur if, for example, a model does not possess capabilities meaningfully different from other publicly available models that have weaker security applied (in which case the marginal benefit of higher security is limited), or if we assess that the benefits of the open release of model weights outweigh the risks.

excerpt: Therefore, we recommend models at this level of capability have exceptional security even though they may have substantial innovation costs.

excerpt: We have in place a well-established and comprehensive internal governance structure designed to ensure the robust implementation of the processes outlined in this Frontier Safety Framework.
paraphrase: An established internal governance structure exists to ensure robust implementation of this Framework's processes.

excerpt: Responsibilities for assessing and mitigating risks are clearly defined and allocated across all levels of the organization.
paraphrase: Risk assessment and mitigation responsibilities are defined and distributed throughout the organization.

excerpt: This includes legal, compliance, and safety reviews with escalation procedures to ensure appropriate oversight.
paraphrase: The structure includes legal, compliance, and safety reviews plus escalation procedures for oversight.

excerpt: The Frontier Safety Framework will be reviewed at least once a year—more frequently if we have reasonable grounds to believe the adequacy of the Framework or our adherence to it has been materially undermined.
paraphrase: The Framework is reviewed at least annually, or more often if its adequacy or adherence to it is believed materially undermined.

excerpt: The process will involve (i) an assessment of the Framework's appropriateness for the management of significant and severe risk, drawing on information sources such as record of adherence to the framework, relevant high-quality research, information shared through industry forums, and evaluation results, as necessary, and (ii) an assessment of our adherence to the Framework.
paraphrase: The review process assesses the Framework's appropriateness using multiple information sources, and assesses adherence to the Framework.

excerpt: Following this assessment, we may:
paraphrase: Lead-in sentence to possible post-assessment actions.

excerpt: Update our risk domains and T/CCLs, where necessary.
paraphrase: Risk domains and T/CCLs may be updated where necessary.

excerpt: Update our testing and mitigation approaches, where needed to ensure risk remains adequately assessed and addressed according to our current understanding.
paraphrase: Testing and mitigation approaches may be updated where needed to ensure risk remains adequately assessed and addressed.

excerpt: The updated version and framework assessment will be reviewed by the appropriate corporate governance bodies.
paraphrase: Corporate governance bodies review the updated version and framework assessment.

excerpt: If we assess that a model has reached a CCL that poses an unmitigated and material risk to overall public safety, we aim to share relevant information with appropriate government authorities where it will facilitate safety of frontier AI.
paraphrase: If a model reaches a CCL posing unmitigated material risk to public safety, relevant information is aimed to be shared with government authorities where it aids frontier AI safety.

excerpt: Where appropriate, and subject to adequate confidentiality and security measures and considerations around proprietary and sensitive information, this information may include:
paraphrase: Lead-in sentence listing potential disclosure content, subject to confidentiality and security considerations.

context_stem: Where appropriate, and subject to adequate confidentiality and security measures and considerations around proprietary and sensitive information, this information may include:
excerpt: Model information: characteristics of the AI model relevant to the risk it may pose with its critical capabilities.
paraphrase: Disclosed information may include model characteristics relevant to the risk posed by its critical capabilities.

context_stem: Where appropriate, and subject to adequate confidentiality and security measures and considerations around proprietary and sensitive information, this information may include:
excerpt: Evaluation results: such as details about the evaluation design, the results, and any robustness tests.
paraphrase: Disclosed information may include evaluation design details, results, and robustness test information.

context_stem: Where appropriate, and subject to adequate confidentiality and security measures and considerations around proprietary and sensitive information, this information may include:
excerpt: Mitigation plans: descriptions of our mitigation plans and how they are expected to reduce the risk.
paraphrase: Disclosed information may include mitigation plan descriptions and their expected risk reduction.

excerpt: We may also consider disclosing information to other external organizations to promote shared learning and coordinated risk mitigation.
paraphrase: Disclosure to other external organizations may also be considered to promote shared learning and coordinated risk mitigation.

excerpt: We will continue to review and evolve our disclosure process over time.
paraphrase: The disclosure process will continue to be reviewed and evolved over time.

excerpt: Introduced CBRN TCLs and outlined mitigation and risk acceptance process.
paraphrase: The 3.1 update introduced CBRN Tracked Capability Levels and outlined a mitigation and risk acceptance process for them.

excerpt: Incorporated the previous exploratory Misalignment risk domain into a combined ML R&D and Misalignment risk domain and outlined mitigation and risk acceptance process for the TCL.
paraphrase: The 3.1 update merged the former exploratory Misalignment domain into a combined ML R&D and Misalignment domain and described mitigation and risk acceptance processes for its TCL.

excerpt: Outlined enhanced level of security for CBRN, Cyber and Harmful Manipulation CCLs to Security Level 2+ to protect against non-state actors and insider threats.
paraphrase: The 3.1 update specified an enhanced Security Level 2+ for CBRN, Cyber, and Harmful Manipulation CCLs to guard against non-state actors and insider threats.

excerpt: Included more detail on our risk management process.
paraphrase: The 3.1 update added further detail to the risk management process description.

excerpt: Included description of our internal governance structure.
paraphrase: The 3.1 update added a description of the internal governance structure.

excerpt: Introduced a glossary.
paraphrase: The 3.1 update added a glossary section.

excerpt: Frontier AI Models or Models: are trained on a large data set, display significant generality, are capable of performing a wide range of distinctive tasks and have high-impact capabilities.
paraphrase: Frontier AI models are defined as large-dataset-trained, highly general models capable of diverse tasks and high-impact capabilities.

context_stem: Frontier AI Models or Models definition
excerpt: Frontier AI models' agentic and reasoning-based general capabilities near or exceed those of other Google models.
paraphrase: Frontier AI models have agentic and reasoning capabilities that approach or surpass those of other Google models.

context_stem: Frontier AI Models or Models definition
excerpt: There may be many different checkpoints and versions of the same model along the entire model lifecycle: we consider checkpoints and versions the same model if their base capabilities stem primarily from the same foundational training run, but will conduct additional testing on new versions as specified in Section 1.3.
paraphrase: Different checkpoints or versions sharing the same foundational training run are considered the same model, though new versions still receive additional testing per Section 1.3.

context_stem: Frontier AI Models or Models definition
excerpt: When we refer to "model" in this Framework, we may be referring to a checkpoint or version of the model.
paraphrase: References to "model" in the Framework may denote a checkpoint or version of that model.

excerpt: CBRN: risks of models assisting in the development, preparation, and/or execution of a chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear ("CBRN") threat.
paraphrase: CBRN risk is defined as models assisting in developing, preparing, or executing a chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear threat.

excerpt: Cyber: risks of models assisting in the development, preparation, and/or execution of a cyber attack.
paraphrase: Cyber risk is defined as models assisting in developing, preparing, or executing a cyber attack.

excerpt: Harmful Manipulation: risks of models with high manipulative capabilities potentially being misused in ways that could reasonably result in large scale harm.
paraphrase: Harmful Manipulation risk refers to highly manipulative models being misused in ways that could plausibly cause large-scale harm.

locator: Glossary / Risk Domains / ML R&D and Misalignment
excerpt: ML R&D and Misalignment: risks of models' ML R&D capabilities or misaligned propensities reducing society's overall ability to manage AI risks.
paraphrase: The ML R&D and Misalignment domain covers risks that models' research capabilities or misaligned tendencies diminish society's capacity to manage AI risks.

locator: Glossary / Risk Domains / ML R&D and Misalignment
excerpt: Such capabilities may serve as a substantial cross-cutting risk factor for several pathways (e.g. through misalignment, misuse or structural risks) to severe harm.
paraphrase: These capabilities can act as a significant cross-cutting factor contributing to multiple pathways toward severe harm.

excerpt: Critical Capability Levels (CCLs): are the main capability thresholds around which we have built the Framework process.
paraphrase: CCLs are defined as the primary capability thresholds underlying the Framework's process design.

excerpt: They represent the capability levels at which, absent mitigation measures, frontier AI models or systems may pose heightened risk of severe harm.
paraphrase: CCLs represent capability levels at which, without mitigations, frontier models could pose heightened risk of severe harm.

excerpt: Tracked Capability Levels (TCLs): are capability thresholds which capture a lower level of risks than our CCLs.
paraphrase: TCLs are capability thresholds representing a lower level of risk than CCLs.

excerpt: They represent the capability levels at which, absent mitigation measures, frontier AI models or systems may pose heightened risk of significant but not severe levels of harm.
paraphrase: TCLs represent capability levels at which, without mitigations, models could pose heightened risk of significant but non-severe harm.

excerpt: Alert Thresholds: are thresholds which we set marginally earlier than our CCLs.
paraphrase: Alert Thresholds are set slightly earlier than CCLs.

excerpt: Crossing these thresholds indicates a CCL may be reached in the foreseeable future, due to the speed of capability progress.
paraphrase: Crossing an alert threshold signals that a CCL might be reached soon, given the pace of capability progress.

excerpt: In particular, they are meant to account for the possibility of models reaching a CCL before the next critical capability assessment cycle.
paraphrase: Alert thresholds are designed to anticipate models potentially reaching a CCL before the subsequent assessment cycle.

excerpt: Inherent Risk Assessments: the process of evaluating the level of risk posed by the model.
paraphrase: Inherent Risk Assessments are the process of evaluating the risk level posed by a model.

excerpt: This is part of the risk management process, and includes material capability change assessments and critical capability assessments.
paraphrase: Inherent Risk Assessments form part of the risk management process and encompass both material capability change assessments and critical capability assessments.

locator: Glossary / Inherent Risk Assessment / Critical Capability Assessments
excerpt: Critical Capability Assessments: determine a model's proximity to T/CCLs through the use of early warning evaluations and other sources of evidence.
paraphrase: Critical Capability Assessments assess how close a model is to T/CCLs using early warning evaluations and other evidence.

locator: Glossary / Inherent Risk Assessment / Early Warning Evaluations
excerpt: Early Warning Evaluations: are evaluations which measure the dangerous capabilities of a model.
paraphrase: Early Warning Evaluations are evaluations that measure a model's dangerous capabilities.

locator: Glossary / Inherent Risk Assessment / Early Warning Evaluations
excerpt: They specifically target the threats and risk scenarios identified through our threat modeling to determine a model's proximity to a CCL or TCL, and they provide the most direct evidence for whether these thresholds have been reached.
paraphrase: These evaluations target threat-modeled scenarios to gauge a model's proximity to a CCL or TCL and provide the most direct evidence of threshold attainment.

locator: Glossary / Inherent Risk Assessment / Material Capability Change Assessments
excerpt: Material Capability Change Assessments: indicate whether a critical capability assessment is required.
paraphrase: Material Capability Change Assessments determine whether a critical capability assessment needs to be conducted.

locator: Glossary / Inherent Risk Assessment / Material Capability Change Assessments
excerpt: These assessments are typically conducted upon the completion of new post-training runs on various checkpoints, and they are primarily aimed at determining whether updated versions of a model have developed material capability increases relative to the last checkpoint subject to a critical capability assessment.
paraphrase: These assessments are typically performed after new post-training runs complete, mainly to determine whether an updated model version shows material capability increases relative to the last assessed checkpoint.

locator: Glossary / Inherent Risk Assessment / Material Capability Change Assessments
excerpt: May also be used to assess whether a critical capability assessment is required of non-frontier AI models.
paraphrase: Material Capability Change Assessments may also be applied to determine whether non-frontier AI models require a critical capability assessment.

locator: Glossary / Inherent Risk Assessment / Material Capability Increases
excerpt: Material Capability Increases: are meaningful new capabilities or material increases in model performance that we believe could materially undermine our justifications for a model's level of risk being acceptable, for example, by reaching a CCL that the previous version of the model had not reached.
paraphrase: Material Capability Increases are significant new capabilities or performance gains believed capable of undermining the justification that a model's risk level is acceptable, such as newly reaching a CCL.

excerpt: Response Plans: are plans put in place when a new alert threshold has been reached to prepare for future models reaching a CCL.
paraphrase: Response Plans are plans activated once a new alert threshold is reached, in preparation for future models reaching a CCL.

excerpt: Central to most response plans will be the application of the mitigations described earlier in the Framework.
paraphrase: Most response plans center on applying mitigations already described elsewhere in the Framework.

excerpt: However, if we assess that risks stemming from the model remain acceptable and model capabilities remain distant from a CCL, the response plan may include updating the alert threshold to ensure the safety buffer remains appropriate.
paraphrase: If assessed risk remains acceptable and the model's capabilities are still far from a CCL, the response plan may instead update the alert threshold to preserve an adequate safety buffer.

excerpt: Deployment Mitigations: are safety measures we implement which are intended to counter the misuse or misaligned expression of critical capabilities in deployments.
paraphrase: Deployment Mitigations are safety measures aimed at countering misuse or misaligned expression of critical capabilities during deployment.

excerpt: They may include safety post-training, input/output/chain-of-thought monitoring and analysis, account moderation, jailbreak detection and patching, user verification, and bug bounties.
paraphrase: Examples include safety post-training, monitoring of inputs/outputs/chain-of-thought, account moderation, jailbreak detection and patching, user verification, and bug bounties.

excerpt: External Deployments: represent model releases to entities outside of Google.
paraphrase: External Deployments are model releases made to parties outside Google.

excerpt: They can include both low-risk external deployments as well as general purpose releases to the broader public.
paraphrase: External Deployments encompass both low-risk external deployments and general-purpose public releases.

locator: Glossary / Risk Mitigation / Low-Risk External Deployments
excerpt: Low-Risk External Deployments: represent small scale and private releases restricted to particular external groups or organizations.
paraphrase: Low-Risk External Deployments are small-scale, private releases limited to specific external groups or organizations.

excerpt: Internal Deployments: represent model releases restricted to Google employees for internal use.
paraphrase: Internal Deployments are model releases limited to Google employees for internal use.

locator: Glossary / Risk Mitigation / High-Risk Internal Deployments
excerpt: High-Risk Internal Deployments: represent model releases restricted to Google employees for use cases with the potential to enable severe threat scenarios (e.g. building internal security infrastructure or automating ML R&D).
paraphrase: High-Risk Internal Deployments are model releases restricted to Google employees for use cases that could enable severe threat scenarios, such as building internal security infrastructure or automating ML R&D.

excerpt: Security Mitigations: are safety measures we implement which are intended to prevent the unauthorized modification or exfiltration of model weights by unauthorized actors.
paraphrase: Security Mitigations are measures designed to prevent unauthorized actors from modifying or exfiltrating model weights.

excerpt: They may include identity and access management practices, and hardening interface-access to unreleased model parameters, among other measures.
paraphrase: Examples include identity and access management practices and hardening interface access to unreleased model parameters, among others.

excerpt: We communicate the level of security we consider appropriate to models which cross our thresholds using the RAND model weight security framework.
paraphrase: The appropriate security level for models crossing thresholds is communicated using the RAND model weight security framework.

locator: Glossary / Risk Mitigation / RAND Security Levels
excerpt: RAND Security Levels: indicate security goals and principles relevant to frontier developers aiming to protect their model weights from various actors - with the strength and type of security measures differing for each category of actor.
paraphrase: RAND Security Levels describe security goals and principles for frontier developers protecting model weights, with measures varying by actor category.

excerpt: See https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA2849-1.html.
paraphrase: Footnote 14 provides a link to the RAND research report.

excerpt: Residual Risk Assessments: the process of evaluating the level of risk that remains after all planned mitigation strategies have been implemented.
paraphrase: Residual Risk Assessments evaluate the remaining risk level after all planned mitigation strategies are implemented.

excerpt: This is part of the risk management process, following a critical capability assessment and the effect of mitigations.
paraphrase: Residual Risk Assessments are part of the risk management process, occurring after a critical capability assessment and application of mitigations.

excerpt: The residual risk should be brought within the acceptable levels, as determined by the T/CCLs as relevant.
paraphrase: Residual risk must be reduced to acceptable levels as defined by the relevant T/CCLs.

locator: Glossary / Residual Risk Assessment / Safety Cases
excerpt: Safety Cases: are an assessable argument showing how severe risks associated with a model's CCLs have been reduced to an acceptable level.
paraphrase: Safety Cases are assessable arguments demonstrating that severe risks linked to a model's CCLs have been reduced to an acceptable level.

locator: Glossary / Residual Risk Assessment / Safety Cases
excerpt: Residual risk assessments will be supplemented with a safety case when a model reaches a CCL, and inform a model's risk acceptance determination.
paraphrase: When a model reaches a CCL, residual risk assessments are supplemented with a safety case that informs the risk acceptance decision.

locator: Glossary / Residual Risk Assessment / Safety Cases
excerpt: For misuse risk, such an argument may be based, for example, on considerations such as the effectiveness of mitigations, the scope of the deployment, what capabilities and mitigations are available on other publicly available models, and the historical incidence and severity of related events.
paraphrase: For misuse risk, a safety case argument might draw on mitigation effectiveness, deployment scope, comparable capabilities/mitigations in other public models, and historical incidence and severity of related events.

locator: Glossary / Residual Risk Assessment / Safety Cases
excerpt: For ML R&D and misalignment risk, such an argument may be based, for example, on considerations such as the effectiveness of mitigations relative to model capabilities, and information pertaining to model propensities and the severity of related events.
paraphrase: For ML R&D and misalignment risk, a safety case argument might rely on mitigation effectiveness relative to model capabilities and information on model propensities and severity of related events.

excerpt: See also, for reference, https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.01420.
paraphrase: Footnote 15 references an arXiv paper for additional context.
